counterexample_statements.claim: Torus inner equator: the shortest route has larger heading amplification than a longer route
counterexample_statements.statement: The shortest geodesic between two points has the least heading amplification

counterexample_statements.claim: Torus outer equator: the shortest route has a smaller focus margin s_c - L (s_c the first zero of j_head) than a longer route

counterexample_statements.claim: Torus (0, 0) -> (2.2, 0): two mirror-image shortest routes tie, so 'the' shortest route is not unique

counterexample_statements.claim: Gaussian bump: a longer route over the top has smaller amplification but passes a conjugate point

counterexample_statements.claim: Reduction order alone flips the sign of a float32 sum whose exact value is +0.25 (the one-thread sequential CPU fold against the GPU-style orders)
counterexample_statements.statement: The sign of a float32 reduction (a pass/fail decision at threshold 0) does not depend on the reduction order

counterexample_statements.claim: Reduction order alone flips the sign of a float64 sum of float64-native cancellation data whose exact value is +0.25 (the sequential fold against the GPU-style orders)
counterexample_statements.statement: float64 reductions are order-robust for sign decisions

counterexample_statements.claim: Atomic completion order alone changes a float32 pass/fail test |S - 0.25| <= 0.01 on identical inputs
counterexample_statements.statement: Atomic completion order cannot change a float32 pass/fail decision on identical inputs

counterexample_statements.claim: Emulated atomicAdd completion orders of identical float32 block partials give distinct sums
counterexample_statements.statement: Accumulating the same block partials yields the same float32 result whatever the atomic completion order

counterexample_statements.claim: A comparison-select maximum (a if a >= b else b, the rule numpy documents for np.maximum) returns its first operand for +0.0 and -0.0, so the sign of the result depends on operand order
counterexample_statements.statement: A max reduction built from a comparison select is bitwise order-invariant for every IEEE input

counterexample_statements.claim: Fused multiply-add contraction of the common workload's in-kernel reductions changes its binary64 outputs, so a bitwise CPU/GPU comparison detects a contracting build
counterexample_statements.statement: A fixed-order reduction gives the same binary64 result whether or not the compiler contracts its multiply-adds

counterexample_statements.claim: ciw.core.identities.canonical_json and ciw.telemetry.canonical produce different bytes for non-ASCII text

counterexample_statements.statement: CIW canonical JSON bytes equal RFC 8785 JCS bytes

counterexample_statements.claim: Rust's own shortest float formatting breaks exact decimal ties away from the specification
counterexample_statements.statement: Rust's shortest float formatting yields the CPython repr digits

counterexample_statements.claim: Fixed-order pairwise summation is reproducible for one order but not permutation-invariant

counterexample_statements.claim: Kahan summation loses the sum [1, 1e100, 1, -1e100] that Neumaier summation keeps
counterexample_statements.statement: Kahan compensated summation is accurate whenever Neumaier's is

counterexample_statements.statement: Neumaier summation error is at most 2u|S| + 4n u^2 sum|x|

counterexample_statements.claim: A resealed relabel of the synthetic energy fixture under a fresh occurrence is accepted by the workbench and classified as a physical-domain measurement
counterexample_statements.statement: CIW energy records can distinguish a genuinely acquired log from a relabelled synthetic fixture

counterexample_statements.statement: CIW's retained records and their classification keep provider-backed results visibly distinct from fabricated ones

counterexample_statements.claim: A paraphrased acceptance statement outside both screened vocabularies, filed in a computational domain with a passing check, is still labelled by its checks
counterexample_statements.statement: The lab API cannot mark production acceptance

counterexample_statements.claim: Ignoring the camera-tracker cross-correlation makes the filter overconfident: run-averaged NEES exceeds the 99% upper bound at nearly every tick
counterexample_statements.statement: Ignoring correlation between sensor noises is harmless

counterexample_statements.claim: The ignored-correlation filter still passes the mean-NIS test (grand mean near 4); among innovation-based tests, which need no ground truth, only the whitened-innovation covariance test exposes the missing cross-correlation
counterexample_statements.statement: A passing mean-NIS chi-square test shows the measurement noise model is correct

counterexample_statements.claim: Assuming a common-mode correlation that the noise does not have makes the filter underconfident (run-averaged NEES below the 99% lower bound at nearly every tick) and less accurate than the block-diagonal filter, while its NIS exceeds the 99% upper bound at nearly every tick: the reverse mismatch is neither harmless nor invisible
counterexample_statements.statement: Assuming correlation between sensor noises where there is none is a conservative, harmless choice

counterexample_statements.claim: Normalizing innovations by the raw sensor covariance R inflates NIS to tr(R^-1 S) and fails the chi-square test at nearly every tick
counterexample_statements.statement: Innovations can be tested against the raw sensor covariance

counterexample_statements.claim: Normalizing post-fit residuals by the raw R deflates them to tr(S^-1 R) < 2, which would hide an inconsistent filter
counterexample_statements.statement: Post-fit residuals have the sensor covariance R

counterexample_statements.claim: On the torus outer equator the separation at the conjugate point scales as eps^3, not eps^2
counterexample_statements.statement: The separation at a conjugate point is of exact order eps^2

counterexample_statements.claim: The relative first-order error diverges like 1/|s - s*| approaching the conjugate point
counterexample_statements.statement: The first-order separation eps j is accurate along the whole path once eps is small

counterexample_statements.claim: After the conjugate point the separation inverts sign and still follows eps j
counterexample_statements.statement: Neighbouring geodesics stay on the side of the base geodesic they start on (the signed separation keeps its sign along the path)

counterexample_statements.claim: Past the conjugate point the first-order prediction recovers: the relative error falls again like 1/|s - s*|
counterexample_statements.statement: Once the first-order prediction has failed at a conjugate point it stays invalid beyond it

counterexample_statements.claim: Separation does not grow monotonically with length: it nearly vanishes at the conjugate point
counterexample_statements.statement: The separation of neighbouring geodesics grows monotonically with length

counterexample_statements.claim: On the unit sphere a pure heading perturbation refocuses exactly: the relative first-order error of the embedded chord is uniform (2 sin(eps/2)/eps - 1, about -eps^2/24) and does not diverge at the conjugate point
counterexample_statements.statement: The relative first-order error diverges at every conjugate point

counterexample_statements.claim: On the unit sphere the image inverts after the conjugate point (signed ratio -1)
counterexample_statements.statement: The image of a family of geodesics keeps its orientation beyond a conjugate point

counterexample_statements.claim: Unit sphere, pure heading: C2 = 0, C3 = -|sin s| cos^2 s / 24, and the domain does not shrink at s = pi
counterexample_statements.statement: The validity domain of the first-order approximation shrinks to zero at every conjugate point

counterexample_statements.claim: Lateral variance collapses at the sphere's conjugate point s = pi: the heading contribution vanishes because j_head(pi) = 0, leaving only the initial lateral variance
counterexample_statements.statement: Lateral position uncertainty grows monotonically with distance travelled

counterexample_statements.claim: The heading standard deviation at which the first-order variance is 10% too large is about ten times smaller on the hyperbolic plane at s = 3 than on the sphere near its conjugate point (s = 0.9 pi)
counterexample_statements.statement: A first-order (Phi P Phi^T) covariance is accurate for any heading uncertainty below 0.1 rad

counterexample_statements.claim: Integer matrices with det != 1 are refused as SL(2,Z) basis changes
counterexample_statements.statement: Any integer change of basis generates the same lattice

counterexample_statements.claim: A binary64 heading slope is rational, so a float simulation cannot represent a non-closing direction
counterexample_statements.statement: A floating-point geodesic direction can be irrational (non-closing)

counterexample_statements.claim: Transporting winding labels with M instead of M^-1 breaks length invariance
counterexample_statements.statement: Winding labels transform with the same matrix as the basis

counterexample_statements.claim: The length spectrum does not determine the oriented shape: a mirror image is isospectral but not SL(2,Z)-equivalent
counterexample_statements.statement: Equal length spectra imply SL(2,Z)-equivalent oriented lattices

counterexample_statements.claim: The adaptive-order checks reject a Dormand-Prince variant that advances with its fourth-order solution
counterexample_statements.statement: An effective order near 5 is observed whatever solution a DP5(4) pair advances

counterexample_statements.claim: No convergence order is observable on flat Cartesian charts: every method is exact to rounding there
counterexample_statements.statement: Every integrator exhibits its nominal convergence order on every surface

counterexample_statements.claim: Unit speed does not certify an accurate path: renormalized Euler keeps |g - 1| at rounding with a first-order endpoint error
counterexample_statements.statement: A computed geodesic whose speed stays exactly 1 is accurate

counterexample_statements.claim: RK4 determinant drift is O(h^5), one order above its O(h^4) global error, on constant and variable curvature
counterexample_statements.statement: The RK4 transfer-matrix determinant drifts at the method's global order h^4

counterexample_statements.claim: Where K = 0 every method preserves det Phi = 1 exactly, Euler included
counterexample_statements.statement: Explicit Euler never preserves the transfer-matrix determinant

counterexample_statements.claim: On variable curvature the first focal point is not half the first conjugate distance
counterexample_statements.statement: The first focal point lies at half the first conjugate distance

counterexample_statements.claim: A curvature-misscaled sphere passes every identity except the Gauss equation
counterexample_statements.statement: Metric symmetry, positive definiteness, Christoffel symmetry, metric compatibility and derivative consistency together certify a surface implementation

counterexample_statements.claim: Metric compatibility cannot detect wrong metric derivatives
counterexample_statements.statement: A metric-compatible connection certifies the metric derivatives

counterexample_statements.claim: Dual-number checks expose a hand-coded derivative defect that symmetry checks cannot see
counterexample_statements.statement: Finite, index-symmetric hand-coded metric derivatives are correct

counterexample_statements.claim: Smaller finite-difference steps can be far less accurate
counterexample_statements.statement: Decreasing the finite-difference step always improves agreement with the analytic derivative

counterexample_statements.claim: Quadratic metrics have no truncation branch and a constant metric differences to exactly zero
counterexample_statements.statement: Every smooth metric shows an O(h^2) truncation branch in central-difference error

counterexample_statements.claim: A single polar chart fails or loses accuracy on great circles passing near its pole
counterexample_statements.statement: Fixed-step RK4 in a single polar chart integrates every great circle as accurately as a chart-switching atlas at the same step count

counterexample_statements.claim: From a declared angular-momentum seed of 1e-12, chart A alone crosses both poles of the meridian at 400 RK4 steps to within 1e-6
counterexample_statements.statement: Fixed-step integration in a single polar chart across its pole always fails

counterexample_statements.claim: Across declared seeds from 1e-15 to 1e-10, chart A alone fails on the meridian whenever an RK4 stage point lands within 0.9 d* of a pole and never beyond 1.5 d*, d* = (L0 h^4)^(1/5), but no single multiple of d* separates the outcomes at every seed (350 to 450 RK4 steps at 1e-12, the step counts within 2 d* at the other half-decade seeds)
counterexample_statements.statement: A single-chart integration that crosses a pole accurately at one step count stays accurate at nearby step counts

counterexample_statements.claim: The scan misses the removable coordinate singularity of the plane in the cube-root chart
counterexample_statements.statement: The scan detects every coordinate singularity, that is every det g -> 0 or cond g -> infinity at finite distance with bounded K

counterexample_statements.claim: The graph z = r^(3/2) has a curvature singularity although its Monge metric is regular
counterexample_statements.statement: A nondegenerate metric chart implies bounded Gaussian curvature

counterexample_statements.claim: Christoffel blow-up and curvature blow-up are independent near singular points
counterexample_statements.statement: Christoffel-symbol blow-up indicates a curvature singularity

counterexample_statements.claim: A cone apex and the polar-chart origin share every pointwise exponent; only the circumference ratio separates them
counterexample_statements.statement: Pointwise metric and curvature invariants distinguish a removable coordinate singularity from a conical point

counterexample_statements.claim: Cases just beyond each classification threshold are misclassified
counterexample_statements.statement: The approach scan classifies every singular point correctly

counterexample_statements.claim: Cartesian loops around the sphere pole in the polar chart make a coordinate singularity read as a conical point
counterexample_statements.statement: The scan classifies a degenerate point independently of the approach loops chosen by the caller

counterexample_statements.claim: Curvature and normals evaluated on an unvalidated zero-area face are nonfinite
counterexample_statements.statement: Curvature and normal formulas can be evaluated safely on unvalidated meshes

counterexample_statements.statement: A fixed face corridor (fixed mesh combinatorics) represents the perturbed marker geodesic at every tested vertex-noise level

counterexample_statements.statement: The strip with the largest vertex margin leaves its fixed face corridor least often at every tested noise level

counterexample_statements.claim: First-order propagation underestimates angle-defect curvature variance at sigma = 1e-2
counterexample_statements.statement: First-order (linearized) propagation of vertex noise is adequate for angle-defect curvature at sigma = 1e-2 on icosphere-3

counterexample_statements.statement: Refining the mesh reduces the error of angle-defect curvature
